title_en: Joseph Moore: The Investments That Matter Most May Not Be in Your Portfolio
title_zh: Joseph Moore：最重要的投资，未必在你的投资组合里
subtitle_zh: 历史学家复盘美国三百年理财建议：出人头地的秘诀一直在变
summary_zh: 本期Morningstar《The Long View》由主持Amy Arnott与Christine Benz对话历史学家、畅销书《How to Get Rich in American History》作者Joseph Moore。Moore以历史学家的视角复盘美国三百年来的理财建议，指出「什么永远管用」其实每一代人都在变，所谓「美国梦已死」的论调早在1670年代就已出现，媒体与政客的唱衰构成一种「绝望工业综合体」（despair industrial complex）。他借Raj Chetty的数据反驳流动性衰退论：出生在最低五分之一家庭的人中，十分之六能在一生中脱离底层，向上流动其实快于祖先。他主张人们应多承担可控的风险，优先投资自己的职业与证书，其次是经营小企业；并强调财富多在「快时间」的爆发中产生，需在「慢时间」里靠流动性与债务期限管理做好布局。他还提出婚姻是财务成功最强的预测指标之一，因为资本主义本质是一项团队运动。这期节目以诙谐而扎实的历史证据，为普通投资者提供了跨越周期的理财视角。

turns.en: Our guest on the podcast today is Joseph Moore, a historian and author of the best-selling book How to Get Rich in American History, 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't, where he chronicles all of the various things Americans have tried to do to get ahead over three centuries.
turns.zh: 今天我们请到的嘉宾是Joseph Moore，他是一位历史学家，也是畅销书《How to Get Rich in American History》（美国历史上的致富之道：三百年里管用过和不管用的理财建议）的作者。在这本书里，他记录了三个世纪以来美国人为出人头地尝试过的种种办法。

turns.en: He's also an investor who went from being an academic to funding a tech startup, buying land on the moon, founding a cryptocurrency and owning dozens of investment properties. So Christine, this was a really fun conversation where we covered a lot of ground about the
turns.zh: 他同时也是一位投资人，从学者一路做到资助科技创业公司、买月球上的地、创立一种加密货币，还持有几十处投资性房产。Christine，这是一次特别有意思的对话，我们聊了很多，涉及到……

turns.en: history of financial advice in the US, as well as Joseph's own adventures in investing and money making ventures. And one of the really interesting things he said, I thought, was that who you marry is actually a really strong indicator of financial success.
turns.zh: ……美国理财建议的历史，还有Joseph本人在投资和赚钱门道上的种种冒险经历。我觉得他说的一个特别有意思的点是：你结婚的对象，其实是财务成功的一个很强的风向标。

turns.en: I really like that part of the conversation to Amy as well as his discussion of the secret role of women in household financial decision-making, also thought Joseph's conversation of what he caused the despair industrial complex was incredibly thought-provoking. Yeah, those were all highlights for me too.
turns.zh: Amy，我也很喜欢那一段对话，还有他谈到的女性在家庭财务决策中不为人知的作用；我还觉得Joseph所说的、他称之为「绝望工业综合体」（despair industrial complex）的那个概念特别发人深省。是啊，这些也都是我眼中的亮点。

turns.en: All right, so let's roll the tape. Joseph, welcome to the long view. I am so excited to be here, thank you for having me. Well, we're excited to have you. You started out as a college professor and I wanted to ask, how did you first get involved in real estate investing and writing about financial history and what gave you the idea
turns.zh: 好，那我们开始播放录音吧。Joseph，欢迎来The Long View。我太高兴能来这儿了，谢谢你们邀请我。我们也很高兴请你来。你最初是位大学教授，我想问问，你当初是怎么开始接触房地产投资、又是怎么走上书写金融历史这条路的？是什么让你有了……

turns.en: to write this book? Dodging a bullet is the answer to that question. So it's 2006, I think, my wife and I were graduate students. And back then, the lesson of history supposedly was clear, everybody told you that the lesson of history was renting, was throwing your money away.
turns.zh: ……写这本书的念头？答案是「躲过了一颗子弹」。那应该是2006年，我和我妻子当时都还是研究生。那时候，历史给出的所谓教训是很清楚的，人人都告诉你，历史的教训就是——租房等于把钱白白扔掉。

turns.en: And instead of thinking about that, like a historian, because I was literally getting a PhD in history as a graduate student, I nodded my head like everybody else did, and we got, we're both graduate students, and we got a no-income, no-verification loan
turns.zh: 而我呢，明明当时正在读历史学博士，却没有像个历史学家那样去思考这件事，反倒像所有人一样连连点头。我们俩都是研究生，结果申请到了一笔「无收入、无核实」（no-income, no-verification）的贷款，

turns.en: to buy a townhouse, which sounds as ridiculous today as it was then, but nobody thought it was ridiculous then. Fast forward 2008, our church offers a personal finance class for families, we went, they made us fill a budget, we go home. My wife goes to sleep, I did not sleep a wink, I literally paced the house all night, because
turns.zh: 去买了一套联排别墅（townhouse）。这事今天听来荒唐，当时其实也一样荒唐，只是那会儿没人觉得荒唐。时间快进到2008年，我们教堂办了一门面向家庭的个人理财课，我们去上了，他们让我们填一份预算，然后回家。我妻子倒头就睡，我却一分钟都没睡着，整整一夜在屋里来回踱步，因为……

turns.en: I was thinking, who gave us a mortgage? Like, we have no business owning anything, and we're graduate students. And so we put our house on the market, it sold on a Saturday, and the reason I remember the Saturdays was the following Saturday, our neighbor put her house on the market and it never sold.
turns.zh: ……我在想，到底是谁批给了我们这笔按揭？我们根本就没资格拥有任何东西，我们不过是研究生。于是我们把房子挂了出去，一个周六就卖掉了。我之所以记得那个周六，是因为紧接着的下一个周六，我们的邻居也把她的房子挂了出去，却怎么也卖不掉。

turns.en: So it was the 2008 Titanic had sunk, and we were the last two people off of it. And I just kind of woke up intellectually and thought, why did I not think like a historian? So I had no business training whatsoever. But I wanted to come at this topic as a historian would, to ask what were people told to do? Did it work?
turns.zh: 所以说，2008年这艘「泰坦尼克号」已经沉了，而我们是最后两个跳下船的人。我在思想上算是猛然惊醒，心想：我当初怎么就没像个历史学家那样去思考呢？我完全没受过任何商科训练，但我想用历史学家的方式来切入这个话题，去问：人们当初被告知该怎么做？那些做法管用吗？

turns.en: And if so, what can we learn from that? And so that began kind of an over-decade long journey of trying to find absolutely every scrap of financial advice I could discover in American history. As it turns out, what everyone thought always worked was always changing.
turns.zh: 如果管用，我们又能从中学到什么？就这样，我开启了一段长达十多年、试图在美国历史上翻遍每一丁点理财建议的旅程。结果发现，人人都以为「永远管用」的那些做法，其实一直在变。

turns.en: And so in every generation, people finally feel like, well, we finally figure it out, finance, and what to do to actually get ahead, and that it changes. And generation by generation, people have to adapt, and that's one of the things that you kind of take away from studying the past, is we think the past is this stable thing,
turns.zh: 于是每一代人都会觉得：好了，我们总算把理财、把「怎么才能真正出人头地」这件事搞明白了——可它又变了。一代又一代，人们都得去适应。研究过去，你会得到的一个体会是：我们总以为过去是件稳定不变的东西，

turns.en: and we are what moves through time. But the mean is moving behind you. And we can learn a lot by seeing how much change other generations had to endure. And I got lucky to endure that change on the right side of the 08 financial crisis. So we wanted to delve into some of the lessons that we can all learn from history.
turns.zh: 而我们才是那个在时间里前行的人；但其实你脚下的地形也在不断移动。看看别的世代不得不承受多少变化，我们能学到很多。我很幸运，在2008年金融危机中站在了对的一边熬过了那次变化。所以，我们想深入聊聊从历史中人人都能学到的一些经验教训。

turns.en: But we wanted to stick with your background a little bit. You decided to use what you know about history to make a million dollars, and you actually succeeded at that. Did you always have a more practical bent than the typical academic? And I'm curious what people in your circle, your academic circle, thought about your
turns.zh: 不过我们还想再多聊聊你的背景。你决定用自己懂的历史去赚到一百万美元，而且你真的做到了。比起典型的学者，你是不是一直都更务实一些？我也很好奇，你圈子里的人、你学术圈的人，是怎么看你这些……

turns.en: money-making efforts. Oh, no, they thought I was crazy, bluntly. So look, I have a lot of dear academic friends who kind of cross all ideological spectrums. But there is a tendency in academia, especially in the humanities where I reside, to think and talk very grandly about the working class.
turns.zh: ……赚钱举动的。哦不，直说吧，他们觉得我疯了。要知道，我有很多亲爱的学界朋友，横跨各种意识形态光谱。但学术界有一种倾向，尤其在我所处的人文学科里——大家喜欢用非常宏大空泛的方式去谈论工人阶级。

turns.en: Very few of the people who make such statements are actually from themselves, the working class. And I was raised in rural South Carolina. You know, I come from where the money was not found. Nobody in my family had money. I didn't know anybody. I didn't know a single person of my entire life until I'd probably was in my 30s who
turns.zh: 而说这些话的人里，真正出身工人阶级的极少。我是在南卡罗来纳州的乡下长大的。你知道吗，我来自一个「钱根本无处可寻」的地方。我家里没人有钱，我谁都不认识。直到我大概三十多岁，我这辈子都不认识哪怕一个……

turns.en: went to Ivy League school. So like, there was just, this was a world apart from most academic backgrounds. I have a fun game I play with myself when I'm in academic conferences. We're sitting around shooting the breeze, drinking a beer or something. And I'll ask people, where did you go to high school?
turns.zh: ……上过常春藤名校的人。所以说，这跟大多数学术圈的出身简直是两个世界。我在学术会议上会跟自己玩一个有趣的游戏：大家围坐着闲聊、喝杯啤酒什么的，我就会问别人：你高中是在哪儿读的？

turns.en: Because they're not ready for that question. They are thinking where did you go to grad school, where did you do your undergrad. And so they'll just tell you, and I'll go look it up, and almost inevitably, it's like the most elite public education school or a preparatory academy somewhere.
turns.zh: 因为他们压根没准备好被问这个问题。他们心里想的是「你研究生在哪儿读的、本科在哪儿读的」。所以他们就直接告诉你，我再去查一查，几乎无一例外，那都是某所最顶尖的公立学校，或者某地的预科书院（preparatory academy）。

turns.en: And I'm like, don't you write books about the working class? But I came here, my father used to climb underneath mobile homes and inspect electrical wire. Like, that was his job. He made $14,000 a year for a long time. And so I was just raised around the trades.
turns.zh: 我就会想：你不是写工人阶级的书吗？可我自己是这么过来的——我父亲过去常爬到活动房屋底下检查电线，那就是他的工作。他很长一段时间里一年只挣一万四千美元。所以我就是在各种手艺行当中长大的。

turns.en: I was raised around guys who, you know, did working class jobs and we had a working class life. And it didn't occur to me to not have those values. And I remember when I got into academia, I was shocked because it was the first time I met people who would tell me without thinking about it, that something was beneath them.
turns.zh: 我身边都是干着工人阶级活儿的人，我们过着工人阶级的生活。我从没想过自己不该有那样的价值观。我记得刚进学术界时我很震惊，因为那是我第一次遇到一些人，会想都不想就告诉我，某件事「有失身份」、配不上他们。

turns.en: Like, I wouldn't do that. That's beneath me. Like, something's, it never occurred to me that something was beneath me to do. And so yes, I do have a more practical bent, I think, than the average, especially humanities academic. And that led me to see things differently.
turns.zh: 就像「那事我不干，那有失我的身份」。可对我来说，从来没有什么事是「有失身份、不该我去做」的。所以，是的，我觉得比起一般人、尤其是人文学科的学者，我确实更务实一些。这也让我看事情的角度不一样。

turns.en: And I think one of the things that's been a joy of this book tour is that in the world of finance, the reason my book is so different is that it, I didn't take any of the financial assumptions for granted that everyone just assumes are there. I asked different questions.
turns.zh: 我觉得这次新书巡回宣传中的一大乐趣在于：在金融这个圈子里，我的书之所以这么与众不同，是因为我没有把大家习以为常、默认存在的那些金融假设当成理所当然。我问的是不一样的问题。

turns.en: From the academic perspective, it never occurred to me that those questions weren't worth asking. And hopefully that's led to a unique, a unique book, certainly, it's been a crazy ride for me. Yeah, definitely is unique and also very funny. So I really enjoyed reading it. Thank you. That was intentional.
turns.zh: 从学者的角度看，我压根没想过那些问题「不值得问」。希望这最终成就了一本独特的书——它肯定是独特的，对我来说也绝对是一段疯狂的旅程。是啊，确实独一无二，而且非常有趣，我读得特别开心，谢谢你。那是有意为之的。

turns.en: I really wanted it to be a fun read. I mean, I, I told somebody, I wanted to write a history of everyday people's finances that everyday people would enjoy reading. And so that's been one of the most rewarding things is here people say they enjoyed it. But it's fun to read because I remember when it was fun to read.
turns.zh: 我真的很想让它读起来有意思。我跟人说过，我想写一部普通人的财务史，而且是普通人自己会喜欢读的那种。所以最有成就感的事情之一，就是听到大家说他们读得很开心。它之所以好读，是因为我记得那些历史本身当年就很好读。

turns.en: So we need more books that are fun to read. Yeah, especially about finance. So one of the very first ideas you introduce in the book is the phrase go ahead. And do you write that this was sort of like a 19th century internet meme that meant moving to a better place than you began?
turns.zh: 所以我们需要更多好读的书。是啊，尤其是讲金融的。你在书里最早抛出的一个概念，是「go ahead」这个说法。你写道，它有点像19世纪版的网络流行梗（internet meme），意思是挪到一个比你出发的地方更好的去处，对吗？

turns.en: Can you expand a little bit on what that phrase means and what makes this idea of going ahead uniquely American? Yeah. So the subtitle of the book is 300 years of financial advice that worked and didn't. And very few people have picked up on that. But the reason I did 300 years was that predates the American Revolution.
turns.zh: 你能不能多讲讲这个说法的含义，以及「go ahead」这种理念为什么是美国独有的？好。这本书的副标题是「三百年里管用过和不管用的理财建议」，很少有人留意到这点。但我之所以取三百年这个跨度，是因为它早于美国独立革命。

turns.en: And to some extent, what is the first uniquely American financial advice? And that advice is basically this. If you look around you in the poverty stricken town in which you live, England, Scotland, later Italy, parts of China, Japan, if you will get on this rickety boat for roughly
turns.zh: 那么，第一条真正属于美国的理财建议是什么？某种程度上说，它基本就是这样的：如果你环顾自己所在的那座穷困小镇——英国、苏格兰，后来是意大利、中国部分地区、日本——只要你愿意登上这艘摇摇晃晃的船，大约……

turns.en: two months, then you can actually have a chance to get on the property ladder and move up with your life and go ahead from where you are to a better place. And your children will have a chance to do the same. Now, that sounds inspiring, you know, on our side of the boat.
turns.zh: ……两个月的航程，你就真的有机会爬上房产阶梯（property ladder）、让生活向上走，从你现在的处境「go ahead」到一个更好的地方。你的孩子也将有机会做同样的事。当然，这话站在我们这一边船上听起来很励志。

turns.en: And if you're on the other side of the boat, that's a risk reward proposition. It's not entirely clear it will work out. And to be clear, there are some people for whom it does not work out. Some of those boats didn't land in places that worked out. But the idea that you could take a risk to move your family from a place that you would
turns.zh: 可如果你站在船的另一头看，这就是一个风险与回报的命题，能不能成并不完全清楚。而且要说清楚，确实有些人的结局并不如意，有些船并没有抵达能改变命运的地方。但这样一种理念——你愿意冒险，把家人从一个你永远……

turns.en: never get ahead to one where your family could actually see a better life at the end of yours was a uniquely American proposition at the time. You had to actually get on the boat and do it. And so that idea pervades the 19th century especially. And people would talk about this in newspapers, in books, in bars, men, women, like people
turns.zh: ……出不了头的地方，搬到一个你的家人真能在你此生尽头看到更好生活的地方——这在当时是美国独有的一个命题。你必须真的登上那条船、真的去做。所以这种理念尤其弥漫在整个19世纪。人们在报纸上、书里、酒吧里谈论它，男人、女人，大家都……

turns.en: said, it's a go ahead culture. They commented on this over and we're a go ahead, not get ahead. We talk about getting ahead like it happens to you. But their assumption was that go ahead was something you had to get up and go do. And this crossed decades and the whole of the 1800s, it was a wide idea, a black idea.
turns.zh: ……说，这是一种「go ahead（勇往直前）」的文化。他们反复评论这一点。我们是「go ahead」，不是「get ahead（被动地出人头地）」。我们谈起「出人头地」时，好像那是会自己降临到你头上的事。但他们的前提是：「go ahead」是你必须起身去做的事。这种理念跨越了数十年、贯穿了整个1800年代；它是白人的理念，也是黑人的理念。

turns.en: I mean, Frederick Douglass, the famous abolitionist, we remember him mostly for his speech, what to the slave is the 4th of July, which is an incredible speech. We teach it to schools. I've taught it. We should continue to teach it. But in his lifetime, that was even close to his most famous speech.
turns.zh: 我是说，著名废奴主义者Frederick Douglass，我们记住他多半是因为那篇演讲《What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July》（对奴隶而言，7月4日意味着什么），那是一篇了不起的演讲。我们在学校教它，我自己也教过，我们应该继续教下去。但在他生前，那甚至算不上他最有名的演讲。

turns.en: Far and away, his most famous speech was called self-made men. And in that speech, now the gender term there is just the term of the time. He means men and women. But the idea of that speech, the crescendo line, is maybe I cannot be president. He says as a black man in the 1870s, but I can be prosperous.
turns.zh: 他最有名的演讲，遥遥领先于其他，叫《Self-Made Men》（白手起家的人）。那篇演讲里，「men」这个带性别的用词只是当时的说法，他指的其实是男人和女人。那篇演讲的核心思想、那句推向高潮的话是：也许我当不了总统——作为一个1870年代的黑人，他说——但我可以过得富足。

turns.en: And you have to think about like everywhere he went, white audiences and black audiences were calling out for that speech. And after he says I can be prosperous, he says our motto is go ahead. And that idea was pervasive and one that we've largely lost. That we think getting ahead happens to you. They thought that you happened to it.
turns.zh: 你得想想，无论他走到哪儿，白人听众和黑人听众都在喊着要听那篇演讲。而在他说完「我可以过得富足」之后，他接着说：我们的格言是「go ahead」。这种理念曾经无处不在，而我们如今基本已经把它丢了。我们以为「出人头地」是会降临到你头上的事，而他们认为是你主动去成就它。

turns.en: So a central idea of the book is that getting ahead or maybe going ahead is easier than ever. But we constantly see headlines about student debt housing affordability, economic decline. And I would say the statistics I've seen on economic mobility in the US are pretty persuasive that it's not really what it once was.
turns.zh: 这本书的一个核心观点是：出人头地、或者说「go ahead」，比以往任何时候都更容易。可我们却不断看到关于学生债务、住房负担能力、经济衰退的头条新闻。我得说，我看到的那些关于美国经济流动性（economic mobility）的统计数据相当有说服力，说明如今的流动性已经不如从前了。

turns.en: But maybe you can talk about that issue, why the media narrative is so negative and often it odds with historical evidence. So there's kind of two ways we can take that conversation. One is the rhetorical conversation and one is the statistic. So let's do the rhetorical first. Okay.
turns.zh: 但也许你可以谈谈这个问题：为什么媒体的叙事如此消极，还常常与历史证据相矛盾。这个话题其实可以从两个角度切入：一个是修辞层面，一个是统计层面。那我们先谈修辞层面。好。

turns.en: Rhetorically I can find people telling you the American dream is dead probably 300 years before I can find the actual phrase American dream, which comes up in the 1930s. In the 1670s, this is 100 years before Hamilton is going to wrap on Broadway.
turns.zh: 从修辞上说，我能在「美国梦已死」这个说法真正出现之前大约三百年，就找到有人在说这话了——而「美国梦」（American dream）这个短语其实是1930年代才出现的。在1670年代——这比音乐剧《Hamilton》在百老汇上演早了整整一百年——

turns.en: In the 1670s, the colonist of Virginia burned their own capital to the ground in anger because no one could get ahead anymore. Okay. So from the very beginning, there's been rhetoric around no one's getting ahead. You arrive too late. There's big speeches on the 1800s saying this.
turns.zh: 在1670年代，弗吉尼亚的殖民地居民一怒之下把自己的首府烧成了平地，因为再也没人能出人头地了。好。所以说，从一开始就有「没人能出头」这类论调——「你来得太晚了」。1800年代就有大型演讲在讲这个。

turns.en: One of my prized possessions is a 1984 best selling book sold nearly 100,000 copies that said that the baby boomers would never be able to afford to retire. And so the rhetoric is very old. I call this big woe, a kind of despair industrial complex. Because there's no clicks for a journalist.
turns.zh: 我的一件宝贝藏品是1984年的一本畅销书，卖出了近十万册，书里说婴儿潮一代（baby boomers）永远都负担不起退休。所以这套论调历史很悠久了。我把这种「大肆叫苦」称为一种「绝望工业综合体」（despair industrial complex）。因为对记者来说，唱衰没有点击量……

turns.en: There's no votes for a politician heck, there's there's no tenure for an academic like me. If I just get up and tell everybody that the world is getting better, but I can have all of those things if I tell you it's getting worse. So there's kind of the people who are giving that message out are actually being empowered
turns.zh: ……对政客来说没有选票， heck，对我这样的学者来说更没有终身教职（tenure）。如果我站起来告诉大家世界正在变好，我什么都得不到；可如果我告诉你世界正在变糟，这些我全都能有。所以，那些散布这种信息的人，其实是被这种信息……

turns.en: by that message to implement their solutions or to monetize their traffic or whatever it is. But you actually end up getting penalized for listening because if you believe no one gets ahead, then you will not take the actions necessary to get ahead. So there's the rhetorical part of it. I plus move to the statistical part of it.
turns.zh: ……赋能的，好去推行他们的方案、把流量变现，或者别的什么。但结果是你这个听众反倒被坑了：因为如果你相信「没人能出头」，你就不会去采取出人头地所必需的行动。这是修辞层面的部分。接下来我再讲统计层面的部分。

turns.en: There's two buckets of those mobility statistics. One of them is wrong. And the other one I will take and use and flip on its head and show that it actually shows it's a lot better than you think it does. The first set of statistics that came out about mobility showed that the 1800s had this
turns.zh: 关于流动性的统计数据分两类。一类是错的；另一类我会拿来用，把它彻底翻转过来，证明它其实说明情况比你想的要好得多。最早那批关于流动性的统计显示，1800年代的美国有过……

turns.en: wildly rapid upward mobility in America and that it's declined ever since. The problem with those statistics is they were almost all taken from Iowa. The thing about Iowa is that it's not really representative of the whole of the United States. It just happened to have a particularly good data set.
turns.zh: ……极快的向上流动，而此后一直在下滑。这些统计的问题在于，它们几乎全部取自Iowa（爱荷华州）。爱荷华的问题在于，它并不能真正代表整个美国，只是碰巧有一套特别好的数据集。

turns.en: And so a lot of the early mobility stats that celebrated how fast people could get ahead in the 1800s and early 20th century and then had the decline of it basically had forgotten about a lot of poor people, especially minorities who are just aren't in the data.
turns.zh: 所以，很多早期的流动性统计，一边讴歌1800年代和20世纪初人们出人头地的速度有多快、一边又说后来这种速度衰退了，其实基本上把大量穷人、尤其是少数族裔给遗漏了——他们根本不在数据里。

turns.en: And so when you combine the actual different demographic data sets, you find that mobility has gotten faster and not slower. Well we forget how impoverished early Americans really were. Then you look at something like the Ross Chetty famous paper in science that talks about
turns.zh: 而当你把不同的人口统计数据集真正合并起来，你会发现流动性其实是变快了，而不是变慢了——只是我们忘了早期的美国人到底有多穷。接下来你再看像Raj Chetty发表在《Science》上那篇著名论文，它谈到……

turns.en: basically mobility of Americans peaked for the generation born right after World War II, that they got ahead of their parents faster than any generation and that it slows down after 1980. Okay, first of all what they're really measuring is moving from the bottom to the middle class
turns.zh: ……基本上美国人的流动性在二战后出生的那一代人身上达到顶峰，他们超越父母的速度快过任何一代人，而在1980年之后开始放缓。好，首先，他们真正衡量的是从底层攀升到中产阶级的过程，

turns.en: and for the chance to go from the bottom to the middle, that is probably true. However, their parents were living through the great depression. So this is a kind of skewed data set. This idea that like, well my parents lived through the worst economic collapse in history and I'm doing pretty well, is it necessary?
turns.zh: ……就「从底层到中产」这个机会而言，那大概是真的。然而，他们的父母是经历过大萧条（Great Depression）的一代。所以这是一套有点被扭曲的数据。「我父母经历了史上最严重的经济崩溃，而我过得还不错」——这种说法站得住脚吗？

turns.en: It's, you know, the reality is the quality of life that we're living today absolutely dwarfs the quality of life of the early baby boomers. So when I look at that stat, I say, okay, what do we see? This is the Chetty data that I'm using. If you look at people born in the bottom fifth, six and 10 will get out in their own lifetime.
turns.zh: 你知道，现实是：我们今天的生活质量，绝对碾压早期婴儿潮一代的生活质量。所以当我看那个数据时，我会说：好，我们看到了什么？这是我在用的Chetty数据。如果你看出生在最低五分之一的人群，其中十分之六会在自己这一生里摆脱底层。

turns.en: That is not perfect mobility, which would be eight and 10, but it's not that far off. Four and 10 make it to the middle class. One and 10 go all the way from the bottom all the way to the top. That is compared to the rest of human history, mind blowing, upward mobility. The flip side of that is downward mobility.
turns.zh: 这算不上完美的流动性——完美应该是十分之八——但也差得不算太远。十分之四能进入中产阶级，十分之一能从底层一路攀升到顶层。跟人类历史上的其他任何时期相比，这都是令人震撼的向上流动。而它的另一面，是向下流动。

turns.en: Of children born in the top fifth, six and 10 will fall out in their own lifetime, which is the exact same as Denmark. So we have a rhetoric around mobility that is kind of skewed to the idea of one generation's experience. But when you pan the camera back out, you look over 300 years of history, Americans are
turns.zh: 出生在最高五分之一家庭的孩子里，十分之六会在自己这一生里跌落出去——这个比例跟丹麦一模一样。所以，我们围绕流动性的那套论调，其实是被某一代人的经历给带偏了。可当你把镜头拉远、纵览三百年历史，你会发现美国人……

turns.en: getting ahead faster than our ancestors could have ever dreamed we could have. You also note that your father hated rich people and it seems like that sort of a growing attitude in the country now. You know, we see lots of resentment toward the wealthy and interest in taxing billionaires, things like that.
turns.zh: ……出人头地的速度，比我们的祖先做梦都想不到我们能达到的还要快。你还提到你父亲仇视富人，而这种态度如今似乎在全国范围内越来越普遍。你知道，我们看到很多对富人的怨愤，还有对向亿万富翁征税的兴趣，诸如此类。

turns.en: Why has hostility toward wealth remained such a persistent part of American culture? So I think there's, I mean, that's a great question, by the way, and just, you know, I don't want to pretend that I'm going to unlock that mystery in a couple of minutes. But I'd probably take it into kind of general ideas.
turns.zh: 为什么对财富的敌意一直是美国文化中如此根深蒂固的一部分？我觉得……顺便说一句，这是个好问题。你知道，我不想假装自己能在几分钟内就解开这个谜。但我大概会从几个大的思路来讲。

turns.en: One is the kind of upward mobility motif that is the American dream or go ahead, as I used to say, there was an empowerment of people at the bottom that was very unusual compared to any other place in the world at the time. And that gave people a voice to decry anything.
turns.zh: 一个是那种向上流动的主旋律——也就是美国梦、或者我常说的「go ahead」。当时社会底层的人获得了一种赋能，这跟世界上任何其他地方相比都极为罕见。而这给了人们发声、去抨击任何事情的底气。

turns.en: We have, I mean, the free press may be honestly part of the answer, just the idea that you lived in a nation where such opinions could be freely expressed without fear of retribution from said elites and rich people was somewhat unique. And so the ability to print those ideas and those complaints, there may have been those
turns.zh: 说实话，自由的新闻界可能也是答案的一部分。仅仅是这样一个事实：你生活在一个可以毫无畏惧、自由表达这类观点的国家，不用担心遭到那些精英和富人的报复——这本身就有些独一无二。而能够把这些想法和这些抱怨印刷出来的能力……这类抱怨……

turns.en: complaints for all of history, but you can't read them very often. I mean, you get the levelers in England and these, but they're, it's not common. But I think the other thing, the reason that we seem to think it's getting more loud today, I think we probably misjudge how local life used to be and how national our media landscape
turns.zh: ……也许贯穿了整个历史，但你不常能读到它们。我是说，英国有过平等派（Levelers）之类的，但并不常见。不过我觉得另一点、也就是我们今天似乎觉得这种声音越来越响的原因，是我们可能误判了过去的生活有多「本地化」，也误判了我们如今的媒体格局有多「全国化」，

turns.en: has become in the sense that most people's experience with the rich was local. It was the local elites that they knew. They may know the Rockefellers exist, but they'd never met one. They've never walked past their park avenue homes and had to like gawk at them and wonder why they have to live in the tiny apartment.
turns.zh: ……在这个意义上：大多数人跟富人打交道的经验都是本地的，是他们认识的那些本地精英。他们也许知道Rockefeller家族的存在，却从没见过其中一个。他们从没走过Park Avenue那些豪宅门口、目瞪口呆地仰望，然后纳闷自己为什么得住在一间小公寓里。

turns.en: Some New Yorkers might, but most people in the country are living a very local life. And now we have a very nationalized media. And so if you go to the previous time that we have an explosion of kind of critiques of wealth from a kind of socialist perspective the way we're seeing now, the last time was
turns.zh: 有些纽约人也许会，但全国大多数人过的都是非常本地化的生活。而如今我们有了一个高度全国化的媒体。所以，如果你回溯上一次出现像现在这样、从某种社会主义视角对财富进行爆炸式批判的时期，那上一次是……

turns.en: a rounded presidency of Eugene Debs and kind of started with the populist angst about the railroads. But what was happening with railroads and radio is an era in which we're nationalizing our economy and our media. So anytime local people are suddenly confronted with narratives about national elites that they'll,
turns.zh: ……Eugene Debs竞选总统那一段前后，并且差不多是从对铁路的民粹式焦虑开始的。而当时铁路和广播身上发生的事情，正是一个把我们的经济和媒体都「全国化」的时代。所以，任何时候，当本地人突然被推到关于全国性精英的叙事面前——

turns.en: I've never met Elon Musk and probably never will, probably won't seem with my own eyes. But I'm very aware of him in a way I would not be if my media consumption and my life was entirely local and most people's lives generally were. One of the book's main ideas is you live most of your life in slow time and that's a quote
turns.zh: 「我从没见过Elon Musk，大概这辈子也不会见，多半也不会亲眼见到。但我对他了如指掌」——这种了解程度，如果我的媒体消费和生活完全是本地的，是不会有的，而过去大多数人的生活大体都是本地的。这本书的主要观点之一是：你一生中的大部分时间都活在「慢时间」（slow time）里，这是一句……

turns.en: you get rich in fast time. Maybe you could talk a bit more about what that means. So most of us don't think a lot about financial history. It's not top of mind for most of us way wake up in the morning. If we ever think about financial history at all, almost certainly it's what I call fast time history.
turns.zh: 「……而你在快时间（fast time）里变富。」也许你可以多讲讲这是什么意思。我们大多数人平时并不怎么思考金融史。它不是我们早上醒来时脑子里最先想到的东西。而如果我们真的会去想金融史，那几乎一定是我所说的「快时间历史」。

turns.en: That's when everything is changing everywhere all at once to quote the movie and a handful of smart people saw it coming. Everybody else got wiped out and you just don't want to be the dumb people. It's always 1929. It's always 2008. And the problem with those histories is not that they're not good and fun.
turns.zh: 那就是「一切都在同时、到处发生变化」——借用那部电影的说法——而少数几个聪明人预见到了，其他所有人都被一扫而空，你就是不想当那批蠢人。它永远是1929年，永远是2008年。而这类历史的问题并不在于它们不好看、不好玩。

turns.en: They are, but they're not written to teach you what to do with your money. They are written to entertain you and they're very good at that. Like you are supposed to flip the page or look at the movie screen and scream, you know, he's behind you. The subprime mortgage lender is behind you, run away from the mortgage like that's
turns.zh: 它们确实好看好玩，但它们不是写来教你怎么打理自己的钱的，而是写来娱乐你的，而且它们非常擅长这一点。就像你本该翻着书页、或者盯着电影屏幕大喊：「它就在你身后！次级抵押贷款的放贷人就在你身后，快从那笔按揭里逃命！」——这就是……

turns.en: what you're supposed to do with those histories and they're very good at that. But they're not there to teach you what to actually do with your money because most of financial history is not fast time. Most changes slow and imperceptible. And by the way, that doesn't mean it's quiet. It could be very loud and fast time.
turns.zh: ……你该拿这类历史做的事，而它们非常擅长。但它们并不是要教你到底该怎么打理你的钱，因为金融史的大部分并不是「快时间」。大多数变化缓慢而难以察觉。顺便说一句，这并不意味着它安静无声。慢时间里也可能非常嘈杂。

turns.en: One of my favorite things to do when I'm giving public talks, I go around like I give talks and, you know, different organizations or whatever. And I will put on the screen two quotes from the New York Times and one essentially says a depression is right around the corner and one says a booming economy is right around the corner.
turns.zh: 我在做公开演讲时最喜欢做的一件事——我会到各地、给不同的机构等等做演讲——我会在屏幕上放出两段都来自《New York Times》的引文，一段基本上是说「大萧条就在眼前」，另一段说「经济繁荣就在眼前」。

turns.en: And I tell people, these are less than three months apart headlines of the New York Times. Now, guess the year. And people will, you know, hands go up, 1939, 19, you know, 2007, 2008, 19, 29, 1930. I tell them it's 1948. And then I ask if anyone can remember anything that happened in 1948 and usually most people
turns.zh: 然后我告诉大家，这两条《New York Times》头条之间相隔不到三个月。现在，猜猜是哪一年。大家就会举手：1939、2007、2008、1929、1930……我告诉他们是1948年。接着我问，有没有人记得1948年发生过什么事，通常大多数人……

turns.en: cannot because it was a very boring historical year, especially for markets. And yet people were screaming in the headlines that boom, our bust was right around the corner. So slow time can be very loud, but most of your life is lived with people being loud and volatility kind of staying within a normal range.
turns.zh: ……都答不上来，因为那是历史上非常无聊的一年，对市场来说尤其如此。可当时人们却在头条上声嘶力竭地喊着繁荣或崩盘就在眼前。所以「慢时间」也可以非常嘈杂，但你一生的大部分时间，都是在人们吵吵嚷嚷、而波动率大致维持在正常区间里度过的。

turns.en: And that's where most of your financial life will be lived. Most of your financial decisions will be made. And it's the decisions you make in slow time that can be stress tested in fast time. And people usually leap ahead in fast time. Any business owner knows this.
turns.zh: 你大部分的财务人生都会在那里度过，你大多数的财务决定都会在那里做出。而正是你在「慢时间」里做的那些决定，会在「快时间」里接受压力测试（stress tested）。人们通常在快时间里实现跃升。任何企业主都懂这个道理。

turns.en: They'll have a phrase something like, you work and you work and you work and nothing happens and then out of nowhere, everything breaks. And that's most financial life. You also argue that people should take more risks. What kind of risks are actually worth taking? Yeah.
turns.zh: 他们会有这样一句话：你干啊干啊干，什么也没发生，然后毫无征兆地，一切突然崩开。这就是大多数财务人生的样子。你还主张人们应该多承担风险。什么样的风险才真正值得去冒？好。

turns.en: So let's first of all, let's define risk because some people can hear that and think, you know, put out a heat lock on the house and put it all on Bitcoin, which is gambling. And the difference between gambling and risk could be summarized simply as, do you have some measurable impact on the outcome?
turns.zh: 那我们首先得给「风险」下个定义，因为有些人听到这话会想：拿房子去做一笔房屋净值信用额度（HELOC），然后全押到Bitcoin上——那是赌博。赌博和风险的区别，可以简单概括为：你对结果有没有某种可衡量的影响力？

turns.en: You know, I can't affect the price of Bitcoin. Nothing I'm going to do will shake it. But I can have some measurable impact on a whole lot of other risks that I take, whether it's an investment property that I'm going to turn around, whether it's an investment
turns.zh: 你知道，我影响不了Bitcoin的价格，我做什么都撼动不了它。但对我承担的许多其他风险，我是能有某种可衡量的影响的——无论是一处我打算翻新转手的投资性房产，还是……

turns.en: in a small business that I'm going to, you know, run better, whether it's a rearrangement of my investment portfolio so that I'm putting away more money than otherwise would. But like, if I have some control over what's happening, then at least it's a risk not a gamble.
turns.zh: ……一笔我打算经营得更好的小企业投资，或者是我对投资组合的重新安排，好让自己比原本存下更多的钱。但只要我对正在发生的事有某种掌控，那它至少是一种风险，而不是赌博。

turns.en: And I think most risk, if you go back through history, the idea that most of your risks worth taking were all in the market would have not made any sense to anyone. Even business leaders would not have understood that. Most of your risks were going to be in your business or your career.
turns.zh: 而且我认为，如果回溯历史，「你值得承担的大部分风险都在金融市场里」这种想法，对任何人来说都是讲不通的。连商界领袖都无法理解这种说法。你要冒的大部分风险，其实是在你的生意或你的职业生涯里。

turns.en: One of the things I think people can misread and much of literature, including in my book I go to be careful is I'm not saying quit your job and go start a small business and risk it all there. There's ways to risk in business and there's ways to risk inside of another business, like taking a salary from somebody else's business.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们可能会误读的一点——很多文献里都有，包括在我书里我也格外小心——是：我并不是说让你辞掉工作、去开一家小企业、把一切都押在那儿。在生意里冒险有很多种方式，在别人的生意里冒险也有很多种方式，比如从别人的企业里领一份薪水。

turns.en: What I think has happened in the course of the last four to five decades is because the baby vimmers have had such a wild, successful run of having their retirement savings make them rich. We have assumed that the way you get rich is by slowly steadily putting money away in low risk assets. That usually did not work in history.
turns.zh: 我觉得过去四五十年里发生的情况是：因为婴儿潮一代（baby boomers）靠着退休储蓄变富，走出了一段极其成功的行情，我们就想当然地认为，变富的方式就是缓慢而稳定地把钱存进低风险资产里。但在历史上，这种做法通常是行不通的。

turns.en: So the risks were taking the first one is in your career. You know, when young people, if I'll talk to young people and they'll say, you know, should I be putting $100, $200 a month away in the stock market? Sure. Sounds like a great idea. But just a quick question.
turns.zh: 所以我们要冒的风险——第一个就在你的职业生涯里。你知道，我会跟年轻人聊，他们会问：我该不该每个月往股市里存100、200美元？当然，这听起来是个好主意。但我先反问一句。

turns.en: Is there a credential that you could go get that would help you in the next five years double your salary? Put your money on that. I mean, I'm at a guy research in the book who's never been to college, makes a fabulous salary because he's gotten every credential in the industry for airline mechanics.
turns.zh: 有没有一张证书，你去考下来之后，能在未来五年里帮你把薪水翻一倍？那就把钱押在那上面。我是说，我在书里研究过一个人，他从没上过大学，却拿着极高的薪水，因为他把这个行业里飞机机械师（airline mechanics）的所有证书都考到手了。

turns.en: And you literally can't take the plane apart and put it back together, which you have to do every so many miles unless he signs off on it. He's doing great because he invested in his career. There's a big difference to the income of an entry-level nurse and a nurse anesthetist.
turns.zh: 飞机每隔一定里程就必须拆开再重新组装，而除非他签字放行，否则你根本不能这么做。他过得很好，因为他投资在了自己的职业上。一名入门级护士和一名麻醉护士（nurse anesthetist）之间的收入差距是巨大的。

turns.en: And so a first and foremost, invest in your career, investing getting better and better so that your income can grow by an exponent. But then there's small business. I mean, that really is one of the ways most decommillionaires and above got to that point was by owning investing in a small business.
turns.zh: 所以，首要的一点：投资你的职业，不断提升自己，好让你的收入能呈指数级增长。其次是小企业。我是说，大多数千万富翁（decamillionaires）及以上级别的人，真正走到那一步的方式之一，就是拥有并投资于一家小企业。

turns.en: And we have more such decommillionaires and above that we've ever had in American history, even adjusted for inflation, by the way. And most of those people are doing very unsexy jobs in industries you've never thought of. Like the Wall Street Journal ran a thing on these men and women who are doing this.
turns.zh: 而且，我们如今拥有的这类千万富翁及以上的人数，比美国历史上任何时候都多——顺便说一句，这还是在按通胀调整之后。这些人大多数干着非常「不性感」的行当，处于你从没想过的行业里。比如《Wall Street Journal》就报道过一群这样做的男男女女。

turns.en: One of whom has a carpet removal company specializing in over the summer carpet removal because schools, when they need new carpet, they've got like 60 days max to pull that off. And you got a whole school. And he's just specialized in removing carpet for schools. And he's worth 10 million.
turns.zh: 其中一个人开了一家地毯拆除公司，专做「暑期地毯拆除」，因为学校要换新地毯时，最多只有大约60天来完成，而你面对的是一整所学校。他就专门做学校的地毯拆除，如今身家一千万美元。

turns.en: And I've interviewed so many people like this in research in the book who are doing things you would have never thought to do. So take the risk in your own career and small business. I think those are risk we're taking. As a financial advisor, you've got your clients back and we've got yours.
turns.zh: 在为这本书做研究时，我采访过很多这样的人，他们干的事是你永远也想不到的。所以，去在你自己的职业和小企业上承担风险吧，我觉得那些才是值得我们冒的风险。作为财务顾问，你有客户在身后撑腰，而我们在你身后撑腰。

turns.en: With Vanguard's actively managed bond funds, you're backed by consistent performance with the low cost edge for an advantage that keeps compounding and compounding and compounding. And sorry, quick break for legal to learn more of this at Vanguard.com slash audio.
turns.zh: 借助Vanguard主动管理的债券基金，你既有稳定表现的支撑，又有低成本优势——这份优势会不断复利、复利、再复利。抱歉，先插播一段法律声明。想深入了解，请访问Vanguard.com/audio。

turns.en: All investing is subject to risk investments and bonds are subject to interest rate credit and inflation risk. Vanguard marketing corporation distributor and compounding and compounding and compounding. Are you backed by institutional quality bond funds, Vanguard?
turns.zh: 所有投资都有风险，投资和债券面临利率风险、信用风险和通胀风险。Vanguard Marketing Corporation为分销商。复利、复利、再复利。有机构级品质的债券基金为你撑腰——Vanguard。

turns.en: So if most wealth is created in occasional bursts rather than a steady march upward, most should investors position themselves for those fast time moments. So that's a great question, too. I'm working on an essay on this from my sub-stack right now. I have it wrestled down, but I want to make it interesting and fun to read.
turns.zh: 那么，如果大部分财富是在偶尔的爆发中创造的、而不是稳步向上的行进中创造的，大多数投资者是不是应该为那些「快时间」时刻做好布局？这也是个好问题。我正在为我的Substack写一篇文章讲这个。我已经把它基本理顺了，但我想让它读起来有意思、有趣。

turns.en: So that's the part. How do you make social sciences equations fun to read? It's not always an easy circle to square. But it basically boils down to this. The equation is going to look something like this. You're going to have volatility, which you can't predict. You're going to have concentration of assets, which you control.
turns.zh: 这就是难点所在：你怎么把社会科学的方程式写得读起来有意思？这并不总是容易两全其美的事。但它基本上归结为这样：这个方程式大致会长这样——你会有波动率（volatility），这是你无法预测的；你会有资产的集中度（concentration of assets），这是你能掌控的。

turns.en: You decide how concentrated your risk profile is. And then the other things you can control outside of that is how much liquidity do you have against how urgent are your debt deadlines? Not the amount of debt you have, but the payment schedule for that debt.
turns.zh: 你决定自己的风险画像有多集中。除此之外，你还能掌控的是：你手上有多少流动性，去对应你债务的截止期限有多紧迫——注意，不是你的债务总额，而是这笔债务的还款时间表。

turns.en: And people who are in different industries know that debt works very differently in different industries. If you have a lot of debt, but it's all in three and a half percent mortgages on rental properties, your debt deadlines are pretty easy to manage. If you've got a balloon note coming due in 18 months, that is much harder to manage.
turns.zh: 身处不同行业的人都知道，债务在不同行业里的运作方式差别很大。如果你有很多债务，但全都是出租房产上3.5%的按揭，那你的债务期限就相当好管理。可如果你有一张18个月后到期的气球贷（balloon note），那就难管理得多了。

turns.en: So a fast time hits when you have a low liquidity and a looming debt deadline, you can get wiped out quickly. And so needing to manage the liquidity versus the deadlines for your debt is one part of that. But the other part is the concentration. Fast time rewards and punishes concentration.
turns.zh: 所以，当「快时间」来袭、而你流动性又低、债务大限又逼近时，你可能很快就被一扫而空。因此，管理好流动性与债务期限之间的关系，是其中一部分。但另一部分是集中度。「快时间」既奖励集中、也惩罚集中。

turns.en: So when fast time comes, when everything shifts, the people who are concentrated in the areas that it's in are the ones who they outperform everyone else because of the concentration when everything shifted and of course the same thing to the downside.
turns.zh: 所以当快时间来临、当一切都发生转移时，那些恰好集中在变化所指向领域的人，会因为这种集中而跑赢其他所有人——当然，在下跌方向上也是同样的道理。

turns.en: And so you have to think very strategically about where do I want to be concentrated when change comes? And when that change comes, especially if it comes the way I wasn't expecting, can I survive it by looking at the relationship to my liquidity and the debt deadlines that I have to carry?
turns.zh: 所以你必须非常有策略地去思考：当变化来临时，我想集中在哪里？而当那份变化真的来了，尤其是以我没预料到的方式来了，我能不能扛过去？这就要看我的流动性与我必须背负的债务期限之间的关系。

turns.en: Again, you can see why it's just struggled to make that essay fun to read. But you just have to understand that financial time and regular time don't work on the same space. So imagine I put on your wrist a regular, perfectly timed wristwatch. And then I take another clock and I take it to the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.
turns.zh: 所以说，你也能明白为什么我那篇文章写着写着就卡住、难以写得有趣了。但你必须理解：金融时间和普通时间并不在同一个尺度上运行。想象一下，我在你手腕上戴一块走时精准、完全正常的腕表，然后我再拿另一只钟，把它放到纽约证券交易所（New York Stock Exchange）的交易大厅里。

turns.en: The one on your wrist is going to tick with everyone else's time. But the one on the stock exchange is going to tick for every normal second of financial activity. On the average month, the clock on your wrist and the clock on the stock exchange are going to roughly call, you know, they're going to align pretty well because there's an
turns.zh: 你手腕上那只，会随着其他所有人的时间一起走。而交易所里那只，会为每一秒正常的金融活动而走一格。在一个平常的月份里，你手腕上的钟和交易所里的钟会大致对上、走得很齐，因为那是……

turns.en: average month with an average amount of up and down. And so they're going to stay aligned. But every now and again, that clock on the stock exchange speeds up incredibly or goes backwards. And so financial time can operate at a different speed than the time of the life you're living.
turns.zh: ……一个平常的月份，涨跌的幅度也平常，所以两只钟会保持对齐。但每隔一段时间，交易所那只钟就会不可思议地加速、或者倒着走。所以，金融时间运转的速度，可以与你现实生活的时间不一样。

turns.en: And so you want to be concentrated in the right places when that happens and you want to be able to survive it if you're concentrated in the wrong places. We also wanted to ask you a couple of questions about the history of financial advice, which you also cover in the book.
turns.zh: 所以当那种情况发生时，你会希望自己集中在对的地方；而万一你集中在了错的地方，你得有能力扛过去。我们还想就理财建议的历史问你几个问题，这也是你在书里涉及的内容。

turns.en: And you argue that financial advice as a profession emerged almost accidentally. There was no job title of financial advisor before 1969. Can you talk about how the profession of financial advice first got started? Yeah, so let's go before the dawn of modern financial industry. Where was most financial advice found?
turns.zh: 你主张，理财建议作为一个职业，几乎是偶然间冒出来的。在1969年之前根本没有「财务顾问」（financial advisor）这个职位头衔。你能不能谈谈理财建议这个职业最初是怎么起步的？好，那我们回到现代金融业诞生之前。那时大多数理财建议出自哪里？

turns.en: And this surprised me because the trail went cold for me as a story. And I'm basically a detective where I'm reading dead people's mail, trying to figure out what happened. And the trail went cold right around 1910, 1912. Where I ended up finding most financial advice before then was in housewife manuals.
turns.zh: 这一点让我很惊讶，因为作为一个故事，这条线索对我来说断了。我基本上就是个侦探——读着逝者的信件，试图弄清当年发生了什么。而这条线索正好在1910、1912年前后断了。我最终发现，在那之前，大多数理财建议都藏在家庭主妇手册（housewife manuals）里。

turns.en: Because the average housewife has to manage the whole family's income and outgo. These magazines are replete with financial advertisements for mortgage companies or investment opportunities. So like women were really active in forming financial ideas that executing them. And that's a part of history has been completely lost.
turns.zh: 因为普通的家庭主妇必须管理整个家庭的收入与开销。这些杂志里塞满了按揭公司或投资机会的金融广告。所以说，女性在形成和执行财务想法上其实非常活跃。而这一部分历史已经被完全遗忘了。

turns.en: Then something happens in 1912. All financial advice before 1912 was kind of easy to understand. Everyone knew what to do. And that basically boiled down to, you know, if you were going to have paper investments, you want to invest in bonds or dividend yielding stocks at about 5% because there was 0% inflation.
turns.zh: 接着，1912年发生了变化。1912年之前的所有理财建议都挺好懂的，人人都知道该怎么做。它基本归结为：如果你要做纸面投资（paper investments），那就投债券或者股息率约5%的股票，因为当时通胀率为0%。

turns.en: And then in 1912, when there's 0% inflation, everything changes. Inflation goes from zero. So 1912, a gallon of milk costs 24 cents a gallon. If I go back in time to 1812, think about 1812 to 1912. In 1812, Napoleon rules France and men wear hose. Like that's a different world than 1912.
turns.zh: 然后到了1912年，就在通胀还是0%的时候，一切都变了。通胀从零开始起飞。1912年，一加仑牛奶卖24美分。如果我回到1812年——想想1812到1912这一百年——1812年拿破仑统治着法国，男人们穿着紧身长袜（hose）。那跟1912年完全是两个世界。

turns.en: And in 1912, inflation goes from 0% to the next year, it goes eight, which is double where we are right now, eight, 1817, 1715 in five years. Prices doubled. There was not a mother, a grandmother, or a great grandmother who knew what to do. And everything that used to work stopped working.
turns.zh: 1912年通胀从0%，到第二年就蹿到8%——是我们现在水平的两倍。8%……1817、1715……五年之内物价翻了一倍。当时没有任何一位母亲、祖母或曾祖母知道该怎么办。所有过去管用的办法都不管用了。

turns.en: And all the things that you used to be told not to do like invest in stocks started to work. And so there's this explosion of financial literature in the 1910s and 20s about how to understand this new world of what to do. Because there's really not anybody to turn to who has mastered this and kind of codified
turns.zh: 而那些过去你被告知「不要做」的事，比如投资股票，反倒开始管用了。于是在1910和1920年代，出现了金融文献的大爆发，讲怎么去理解这个新世界、该怎么做。因为当时真的没有人可以求助——没人真正掌握了这套东西、把它……

turns.en: it into a job description where they help you. You can go to your banker and they can help you execute some things. You can go to a broker, but most people don't have brokers and most people don't buy stocks. That starts to shift in the 1960s. Most people's financial purchases were one of two things.
turns.zh: ……编纂成一份职业说明、来帮你打理。你可以去找你的银行家，他们能帮你执行一些操作；你可以去找经纪人（broker），但大多数人没有经纪人，大多数人也不买股票。这种情况到1960年代才开始转变。大多数人的金融购买无非两类。

turns.en: If it was a market or put aside real estate, which was actually what most people spent with their money on or invested their money with. But let's go to the paper investments. It was mutual funds and insurance. That's what most people did. And in the late 1960s, there were all kinds of scandals about just how egregious some
turns.zh: 如果把房地产放在一边——那其实是大多数人真正花钱或投资的地方——那么单看纸面投资，就是共同基金（mutual funds）和保险。这就是大多数人做的事。而到了1960年代末，出现了各种丑闻，揭露有些……

turns.en: of the sales techniques were for basically selling insurance products that were mostly good for the insurance company and selling mutual funds with huge fees. I mean, fees that would make mutual fund advisors today feel embarrassed if they got. And while that was great for the industry, it was bad for the average consumer.
turns.zh: ……销售手法有多离谱：卖的保险产品基本上只对保险公司有利，卖的共同基金费用高得吓人——我是说，那种费用要是今天的共同基金顾问收了，都会觉得脸红。这对行业是好事，但对普通消费者却是坏事。

turns.en: And a group of mutual fund salesmen and insurance salesmen agree to have a meeting at the Chicago O'Hare Airport. And I can't where exactly how many it's not many. It's maybe a dozen or so people fly in. These are like the top selling mutual fund and insurance salesmen in the country.
turns.zh: 于是一群共同基金销售员和保险销售员商定在芝加哥O'Hare机场开个会。我说不清确切人数，不多，大概十来个人飞过去。他们都是全国业绩最顶尖的共同基金和保险销售员。

turns.en: And they all feel like this industry is kind of getting rotten and they don't want to be associated with that. So they fly in. They have a meeting and they decide we're going to found a new entity, a nonprofit that's going to be financial advising. So they fly in as insurance salesmen and mutual fund salesmen and they never leave O'Hare
turns.zh: 他们都觉得这个行业正在腐烂，不想跟它扯上关系。于是他们飞过去、开了个会，决定要创立一个新的实体——一个非营利组织，专门做财务咨询。所以说，他们以保险销售员和共同基金销售员的身份飞进O'Hare，却从没以那个身份离开O'Hare——

turns.en: by the way. And then they fly out and they're financial advisors like that's a change they change their title in that meeting and going forward that idea spreads that you could have certified financial planners or financial advisors different groups spring up to do it. But that's a new thing in the 60s.
turns.zh: ……顺便说一句。然后他们以「财务顾问」的身份飞了出来。就在那场会议上，他们改了自己的头衔。此后这个理念传开了：你可以有注册理财规划师（certified financial planners）或财务顾问，不同的团体纷纷冒出来做这件事。但这在60年代还是个新事物。

turns.en: And in a way, I argue it's actually a really good thing because prior to that, you couldn't really find anybody in your local community. Who could help you understand all of these different financial investments all at the same time? So it's a new profession because it's an entirely new investing world.
turns.zh: 而在某种意义上，我认为这其实是件非常好的事。因为在那之前，你在自己的本地社区里根本找不到一个人，能同时帮你搞懂所有这些不同的金融投资。所以这是一门新职业，因为它对应的是一个全新的投资世界。

turns.en: You write in the book that Dave Ramsey has changed more people's personal finances than maybe anyone in history. So why do academics and financial experts tend to look down on figures like Ramsey? Well, I've always loved Morningstar. So something tells me that the Morningstar audience is not going to like that because you've
turns.zh: 你在书里写道，Dave Ramsey改变的普通人个人财务，也许比历史上任何人都多。那为什么学者和金融专家往往看不起Ramsey这样的人物？嗯，我一直很喜欢Morningstar。所以我有种预感，Morningstar的听众不会喜欢这个说法，因为你们……

turns.en: got some very sophisticated financial listeners out there. So let me make my case for why gurus get a bad rap, especially amongst professionals. Finance professors have incredible equations that work very well on spreadsheets. What gurus have is the awareness that Super Bowl ads work.
turns.zh: ……有一批非常老练的金融听众。那让我来陈述一下我的理由，讲讲为什么「理财大师」（gurus）名声不好，尤其是在专业人士中间。金融学教授有一些了不起的方程式，在电子表格上跑得很好；而这些大师拥有的，是「超级碗（Super Bowl）广告有用」这种觉悟。

turns.en: Birthday sex leads to baby number three and I have yet to see a finance equation that models accurately a midlife crisis or a child with special needs. When you live in the real world and it's dynamic and changing, you need some rules of thumb. And what you find when you look at studies of what people who read personal finance gurus
turns.zh: 生日夜的激情会带来第三个孩子——而我至今还没见过哪个金融方程式能准确刻画一场中年危机，或者一个有特殊需求的孩子。当你活在真实世界里，它是动态、不断变化的，你就需要一些经验法则（rules of thumb）。而当你去看那些研究、去研究读过个人理财大师作品的人……

turns.en: actually remember, it's not what's in the book. It's what do you remember from the book? And if I go to the average person who read a finance guru, let's just pick one off the shelf that's particularly egregious rich dad toward dad, which I think we can all agree is an eye role level book.
turns.zh: ……究竟记住了什么时，你会发现，记住的并不是书里的内容，而是「你从书里记住了什么」。如果我随便找一个读过理财大师作品的普通人，我们就从书架上挑一本尤其离谱的——《Rich Dad Poor Dad》（富爸爸穷爸爸），我想大家都同意这是本让人翻白眼的书。

turns.en: The average person only remembers that they should buy assets and that assets are defined very simply as things that make you money instead of cost you money. That's what they actually remember. Now as a thing to remember, that's not such a bad thing, right?

turns.en: And so if you look at the way people read gurus versus what gurus say, there's a disparity. And that disparity really matters. So let's look at Dave Ramsey and every single academic discipline has a paper somewhere in a journal and I'm not making this hypothetically.
turns.zh: 所以，如果你把人们读大师作品的方式，跟大师们实际说的话对比，就会发现二者有落差。而这个落差真的很重要。那我们来看看Dave Ramsey。每一个学科都在某本期刊上有一篇论文——我不是在打假设性的比方。

turns.en: I have read these papers that condemns Dave Ramsey, sociology, women's and gender studies, history, finance, economics. They all have an anti-Dave Ramsey paper somewhere. And sure, there's plenty of things that Dave Ramsey says that I could disagree with.
turns.zh: 我真读过这些谴责Dave Ramsey的论文：社会学、女性与性别研究、历史学、金融学、经济学，它们都各有一篇「反Dave Ramsey」的论文藏在某处。当然，Dave Ramsey说的很多话我也可能不同意。

turns.en: But a German economics student who did not have a dog in the fight who was just looking for an interesting thesis to write, I think it was his PhD thesis. I had the idea to overlay credit card balances with where the Ramsey show, which was an AM radio show through the 90s and 2000s, which show up in a new market.
turns.zh: 但有一个德国经济学学生，跟这场争论毫无利害关系，只是想找有意思的题目来写——我想那是他的博士论文。他想到一个办法：把信用卡余额数据，跟Ramsey节目（一档在1990和2000年代播出的AM广播节目）新登陆某个市场的时点叠在一起看。

turns.en: In other words, when a new radio station would pick the show up, did it change anything? Low and behold, credit card spinning went down in that metro 1.3%. Well, how do you know correlation is not causation or all those things? He has the idea to realize AM radio waves cannot penetrate mountains.
turns.zh: 换句话说，当一家新电台开始转播这个节目时，有没有带来什么改变？结果你猜怎么着，那个都会区的信用卡欠款下降了1.3%。那你怎么知道这不是「相关不等于因果」那一类问题呢？他想到一个点子：AM无线电波无法穿透山脉。

turns.en: Therefore, the zip codes on the other side of mountain ranges won't get the show. They won't get the signal. And sure enough, the credit card spinning data there stays the same. So if you do the math on that, which I have, that means that over the course of his life,
turns.zh: 因此，山脉另一侧的那些邮编区域收不到这个节目、收不到信号。而果然，那里的信用卡欠款数据保持不变。所以如果你据此算一算——我算过——那就意味着，在他这一生中，

turns.en: Dave Ramsey has saved the American economy, the GDP of a mid-size nation state just by yelling at people to sell the car. turns.zh: ……Dave Ramsey仅仅靠冲着人们喊「把车卖了」，就为美国经济省下了相当于一个中等民族国家GDP的钱。当然，这个说法的细枝末节你可以同意也可以不同意。但我倒要看看，你能不能证明你也能为美国经济省下相当于一个中等民族国家GDP的钱。

turns.en: And then concentrate most of those benefits to average working class Americans. That's a pretty hard trick to pull off. And so if you step back and ask what is the effect of these folks versus what is the image of them as TikTok gurus selling scammy courses, they've actually had quite a big impact for the good.
turns.zh: ……而且还能把这些好处的大部分集中惠及普通的工人阶级美国人。这可是个相当难玩的把戏。所以如果你退一步，把他们实际起到的作用，跟他们被塑造成「在TikTok上卖骗人课程的大师」这种形象做个对比——他们其实带来了相当大的正面影响。

turns.en: Now, I tell people don't buy their seminars. Just everything they say that's good is usually for free. And so you don't need to do much more than take what's for free. turns.zh: 不过我告诉大家，别去买他们那些研讨会课程。他们说的所有好东西通常是免费的，所以你不用做别的，把免费的拿来就够了。你在开头谈过你第一次买房地产、并且正好在金融危机前夕拿到贷款的经历。

turns.en: We also wanted to touch on some of your other adventures in investing. You once invested in a West Coast startup that developed technology to help ALS patients communicate, but you ended up losing your entire investment. Lesson, did you take away from that experience?
turns.zh: 我们还想聊聊你在投资上的其他一些冒险。你曾投资过一家西海岸的创业公司，它开发帮助ALS（渐冻症）患者沟通的技术，但你最后把整笔投资都亏光了。你从那次经历里吸取了什么教训？

turns.en: Well, from that one in particular, and I just have so much admiration for the young people who started that business. But what I took away was it's really hard to have a successful business. Like successful business is hard. And anyone listening to this who's run a business understands that anyone who's, I was
turns.zh: 就那一次而言——我对创办那家公司的年轻人真是佩服得五体投地。但我得到的教训是：要成就一门成功的生意真的太难了。成功的生意就是难。任何听过这期节目、又经营过企业的人都懂这一点。任何人……我当时……

turns.en: joking with somebody recently, they said, what turns you from a lefty humanities professor to a kind of moderate conservative kind of pro-capitalism guy? And I said, making payroll. If you've ever had to make payroll, if you've ever actually had to sell enough of a product
turns.zh: ……最近跟人开玩笑，他问我：是什么让你从一个左翼人文学科教授，变成一个偏温和保守、支持资本主义的人？我说：发工资。如果你曾经不得不按时发出工资，如果你真的不得不卖出足够多的产品，

turns.en: of any kind or provide a service of any kind that you are paid for, knowing that you have to put that in the bank because other people are going to pay their bills, the people who work for you are going to pay their bills from that. You get real aware of how hard it is to run a business.
turns.zh: ……不管是哪种产品，或者提供某种能换来报酬的服务，并且心里清楚你必须把钱存进银行，因为别人要靠它付账单——为你工作的人要靠它付他们的账单——你就会真切地体会到，经营一家企业有多难。

turns.en: And those young people did an incredible thing, made an incredible product. But as it turns out, making an incredible product is not enough. You actually have to make an incredible product that the market will reward and do it on a sustained basis. And that's much more difficult. Now, I did a lot of self experimentation for the book.
turns.zh: 那些年轻人做成了一件了不起的事，做出了一个了不起的产品。但结果证明，做出一个了不起的产品还不够。你实际上得做出一个市场愿意买单的了不起产品，而且要能持续地做下去。这就难得多了。为了这本书，我做了大量自我实验。

turns.en: Like the whole idea that I had about maybe five years in, four years in was, okay, I realized I was kind of making a recipe book of all the things Americans had whipped up to try to get ahead, not just become middle class, but like go from where they were to where they dreamed of being.
turns.zh: 大概到第四、第五年的时候，我的整个想法是这样的：好，我意识到自己其实在编一本「食谱」，收录美国人为了出人头地而琢磨出的所有办法——不只是成为中产，而是从他们现在的处境，走到他们梦想中的位置。

turns.en: And so, all right, well, if it's going to be a recipe book, I need to like eat the cooking. So every thing I could find in the past that people did, I would try the present. And the only line that was drawn was my wife saying, under no circumstances. But everything below that line, I tried.
turns.zh: 所以，好吧，既然它要是一本食谱，那我就得亲自「尝尝这道菜」。凡是能在过去找到的、人们做过的办法，我都会在当下试一遍。唯一划下的红线，是我妻子说「无论如何都不行」的那些。而红线以下的一切，我都试了。

turns.en: And one of them was angel investing, right, because that was obviously a big, a big part of how we, how we imagine the 90s and 2000s is kind of these angels investors finding these startups investing in them before adding wealth could and making tons of money. And as it turns out, picking the angels is harder than it looks.
turns.zh: 其中一项就是天使投资（angel investing），因为那显然是我们想象中1990和2000年代的一大组成部分——那些天使投资人找到创业公司、在它们腾飞前就投进去，然后大赚一笔。结果发现，挑中「天使」比看上去要难得多。

turns.en: So, you also tried shorting stocks recommended by Jim Kramer. Can you talk about that experiment and whether it was educational, profitable or just kind of good for laughs? It was all three. Yeah. Yeah. So there's an economics paper, and I keep it more exactly what you're at came out that
turns.zh: 你还试过做空Jim Cramer推荐的股票。你能不能谈谈那个实验？它是有教育意义、能赚钱，还是只是图一乐？三样都占。是啊是啊。有一篇经济学论文——我记不太清确切内容了——它指出，

turns.en: showed that Jim Kramer showed mad money under a very strict set of criteria, and I need to emphasize that point because I don't want anybody to hear this and just go shorting everything Jim Kramer says, but under a very strict set of criteria, when Jim Kramer
turns.zh: ……在一套非常严格的标准下，Jim Cramer在《Mad Money》节目里的表现是可被利用的。我得强调这一点，因为我可不希望谁听了之后，就去把Jim Cramer说过的每只股票都做空。但在一套非常严格的标准下，当Jim Cramer……

turns.zh: ……在他的节目《Mad Money》上推荐买入某只股票时，你可以反手做空它，因为它会先冲高50到55天，然后回落地面。而在那50到55天里，你就可以做空它。既然我把自己找到的每样东西都在试，我就决定也试试这个。

turns.en: And for three months of my life, I sat glued to a television, waiting for all of those factors to align, which it occasionally did. And then I would rush over to the computer and try to short the stock. Believe it or not, I actually beat the market. Now, net of fees, because you got to be around, I'm using a, I had a history professor
turns.zh: 我人生中有三个月，一直死守在电视机前，等着所有那些条件凑齐——偶尔真会凑齐。然后我就冲到电脑前，试着做空那只股票。信不信由你，我还真跑赢了大盘。当然，是扣费前——因为你得一直在场盯着。我用的是一个……我拿着历史学教授的……

turns.en: salary. I don't know if anybody has ever told you this, we don't make a lot of money. History professors get paid in prestige, you know, or all professors really, right? turns.zh: ……薪水。不知道有没有人跟你说过，我们挣得不多。历史学教授拿的是「声望」当报酬，其实所有教授都差不多，对吧？所以我拿着我这点微薄的教授薪水——实际上动用的是我女儿上大学的钱——押到了这场赌博上。

turns.en: And what I learned in that is I actually did beat the market, net of fees I lost. But while Kramer was yelling at me like I was a child and setting off alarm sirens that were bothering my wife and family, I heard my wife holler for the downstairs, come quick, she's doing it. turns.zh: 我从中学到的是：我确实跑赢了大盘，可扣掉费用后我亏了。而就在Cramer像训小孩一样冲我大喊、触发那些吵得我妻子和家人不安的警报声时，我听见妻子在楼下喊：快来，她做到了！而我错过了女儿迈出人生第一步。所以说，我跑赢了大盘。

turns.en: Was it worth it? And the point that I try to make in the book, but it being educational is actually there's this all this rhetoric around you can't beat the market. So don't try. I actually find that literature to be pretty paper thin. I know there's a lot of those studies, what they're actually measuring is professional
turns.zh: 这值得吗？我想在书里表达的那个点——它有教育意义——其实是：围绕「你跑不赢大盘，所以别试了」有各种各样的论调。我真的觉得那些文献站不住脚、单薄得很。我知道有很多那类研究，它们真正衡量的是专业……

turns.en: money managers ability to meet the market, which is a very different thing than saying you can't because professional money managers are operating in a very constrained environment. And bluntly, if you can't beat the market, then Warren Buffett doesn't exist.
turns.zh: ……资金管理人「追平大盘」的能力，这跟「你不可能跑赢」是两码事，因为专业资金管理人是在一个约束极强的环境里运作的。而且说白了，如果人真的跑不赢大盘，那Warren Buffett就不该存在。

turns.en: You actually, there's another study that shows that certain money managers, especially managing $600 million more, do tend to beat the market by about one half of 1%. Which if you multiply that by $600 billion is a ton of money. But if you take the average 401K balance and you tried to do what that many manager does,
turns.zh: 实际上，还有另一项研究显示，某些资金管理人——尤其是管理6亿美元以上的——确实往往能跑赢大盘约0.5%。如果你把0.5%乘以6000亿美元，那是一大笔钱。但如果你拿普通401(k)账户的余额，去试着做那位经理人所做的事，

turns.en: which by the way you can't, let's just imagine. Which is, you know, you got to go to Yale for four years and pay tuition. You've got to work a grueling internship. And then you need to work 70 to 80 hour work weeks. You would eke out an additional $500 a year for the average Americans for a 1K balance. Not the gains that you make.
turns.zh: ……顺便说一句，你其实做不到，我们就姑且想象一下。也就是说，你得去Yale读四年书、交学费，得熬过一份累死人的实习，然后还得每周工作70到80个小时。这样一个普通美国人的401(k)余额，一年也就能勉强多挣出500美元——注意，这不是你赚到的总收益。

turns.en: The extra 500 is what you get for all the 80 hour work weeks. Well, that's one night in a hotel in Miami and Hurricane season. It's not worth it. And so I try to tell people, can you beat the market? Sure. Do you want to? Probably not. You want to get the market to beat your own personal goals. And that's good enough for most people.
turns.zh: 那多出来的500美元，就是你所有「每周80小时」换来的报酬。呃，那还不够在飓风季去Miami住一晚酒店。不值得。所以我总想告诉大家：你能跑赢大盘吗？能。你想跑赢吗？多半不想。你真正想要的，是让市场帮你实现你自己的个人目标。对大多数人来说，这就足够了。

turns.en: Another interesting point in the book is that stocks haven't always been good long term investments. And if you look at history up until about 1862, there were some extended periods when stocks actually had negative returns and bonds outperformed. Why is that part of market history largely ignored? Yeah.
turns.zh: 书里另一个有意思的点是：股票并不总是好的长期投资。如果你看1862年之前的历史，有些相当长的时期里，股票其实是负回报，而债券跑赢了。为什么这部分市场历史在很大程度上被忽略了？

turns.en: So I think it's largely ignored because it's not a very good story. So we have a story that we want to be true. So that's the story we tell. And Jeremy Segal came out with his book, you know, Stocks for the Long Run. And that was a story everyone wanted to hear.
turns.zh: 我觉得它在很大程度上被忽略，是因为这不是一个好听的故事。我们心里有一个希望它成真的故事，于是就讲那个故事。Jeremy Siegel出了他那本书，《Stocks for the Long Run》（股市长线法宝），那是个人人都想听的故事。

turns.en: And look, I'm not trying to throw shade on Segal's book at all, but the reality is it was a very good book for the data set he used, but the data set he used was not complete. Why was it not complete? Because it's actually really hard to know what all the stocks and the returns were for all of American history.
turns.zh: 话说回来，我绝不是在贬低Siegel那本书，但事实是：就他所用的那套数据集而言，那是本很好的书，只是那套数据集并不完整。为什么不完整？因为要弄清整个美国历史上所有股票及其回报，其实真的非常难。

turns.en: Let's start with the fact that Wall Street wasn't the Wall Street we think of today. There were probably a dozen plus stock markets that were actively trading stocks. And not all the stocks in one trade and all know all the others. There was a stock market in Connecticut, obviously it was one Chestnut Street in Philadelphia.
turns.zh: 先从一个事实说起：当年的Wall Street并不是我们今天想到的那个Wall Street。当时大概有十几家以上活跃交易股票的市场，而且并非所有股票都在一个市场交易、也不是人人都知道其他市场。Connecticut有一个股票市场，Philadelphia的Chestnut Street显然也有一个。

turns.en: There's one in South Carolina. One of the most active was Nanshez Mississippi. But no one goes back and looks at the Nanshez Mississippi stock market to see what the returns were because in the Long Run, they were pretty abysmal. So when you actually piece together all the stocks you could buy for all of American history,
turns.zh: South Carolina有一个。最活跃的市场之一是Mississippi的Natchez。但没人回头去看Natchez股票市场的回报如何，因为从长期看，那回报相当惨淡。所以，当你真正把整个美国历史上所有能买到的股票拼凑起来，

turns.en: it turns out bonds beat stocks for most of the 1800s. They were tied until about World War II and stocks had been beating bonds ever since except for a few 15 plus year periods when a few moments when bonds outperformed. What does that mean? It means that stocks for the Long Run is true, but only as old as our last two presidents.
turns.zh: ……结果发现，在1800年代的大部分时间里，债券都跑赢了股票。二者大约一直打平到二战前后，此后股票就一直跑赢债券，只有少数几段15年以上的时期、少数几个时刻债券占了上风。这意味着什么？意味着「股市长线法宝」是真的，但这个「真」的年头，只跟我们最近两任总统一样长。

turns.en: And that is not a universal law of history. I'm a historian. In my line of work, we call that a rounding error. So 80 years is a lot of time, but it's not enough time to know exactly how things will always work going forward. Now I'm not trying to say invested bonds over stocks. That's not what I'm saying.
turns.zh: 而那并不是一条放之四海的历史规律。我是历史学家，在我们这一行，我们把这叫作「舍入误差」（rounding error）。80年是很长一段时间，但还不足以让我们确切知道未来事情会永远如何运作。我并不是要说「该投债券而不是股票」，那不是我的意思。

turns.en: I'm just pointing out people have an illusion of history that is an illusion. And we would do better, just be frank about the fact that every historical era is different. Work in different historical areas was different. So let's not try to learn the lessons of 1850 as if that's a stock market strategy we
turns.zh: 我只是想指出，人们对历史抱有一种错觉——那确实是错觉。我们不如坦然承认：每个历史时代都不一样，在不同历史时期，运作方式也不一样。所以，别去把1850年的经验教训当成一套我们今天……

turns.en: can employ today, because they lived in a very different world than you live in. turns.zh: ……还能用的股市策略，因为他们生活在一个与你截然不同的世界里。你最有说服力的发现之一是：从历史上看，婚姻一直是财务成功最好的预测指标之一。那你能不能谈谈你是怎么得出这个结论的，以及什么样的特质成就一段财务上成功的婚姻？好问题。

turns.en: I arrived at that because you couldn't avoid it when you looked. If you actually look at the financial advice people were receiving for most of history, a lot of it was intertwined as marriage advice. This is true for men and women, by the way. And I actually think this holds all the way to the present day.
turns.zh: 我得出这个结论，是因为你一去看就无法回避它。如果你真去看历史上大多数时候人们所接受的理财建议，会发现其中很多都跟婚姻建议交织在一起。顺便说，这对男人和女人都成立。而且我真的认为这一点一直延续到今天。
