turns.zh: 事实上，有一本很棒的书——哦，书名一下子从我脑子里溜走了，我等会儿要因为报不出书名而懊恼了——那本很棒的书考察了一些现代的亿万富翁，那些不太出名的亿万富翁、非常成功的Wall Street投资人，问他们的人生，然后……

turns.en: says, what's the through line? Like, what are the real lessons you take away? It's almost every one of them says their spouse. This spouse to this day is a strong indicator of financial success. So if you go to the history books, it's everywhere. People were talking about the financial wisdom of the right kind of marriage.
turns.zh: ……问：那条贯穿始终的主线是什么？你真正得到的教训是什么？几乎每一个人都会说：是他们的配偶。直到今天，配偶依然是财务成功的一个强有力的指标。所以如果你去翻历史书，这一点无处不在。人们一直在谈论「选对婚姻」所蕴含的财务智慧。

turns.en: If you go to the 1840s, there's this card game. I don't know. I have kids. And one of the things that's a great joy of parenting is forcing your kids to play again. They don't want to play because you as a parent have something you want to teach them.
turns.zh: 如果你回到1840年代，有这样一个纸牌游戏。我不知道……我有孩子。做父母的一大乐趣，就是逼着孩子玩那些他们不想玩的游戏——只因为你这个当爹妈的有东西想教他们。

turns.en: And there's this card game in the 1840s where you would play as a family at night and you're trying to draw the cards that will give the winner is the person who has the best spouse and you're drawing characteristics of a spouse as you go. And parents are making their kids play this game because they're trying to teach them,
turns.zh: 1840年代就有这么个纸牌游戏，晚上一家人一起玩，你要去抽那些牌——赢家是拥有「最好配偶」的那个人，而你抽的是一张张配偶的特质。父母逼着孩子玩这个游戏，是因为他们想教孩子：

turns.en: like maybe the bad breath card is not so bad if you also are holding the work ethic card. So it was so important to parents to teach young people this. If you go into the novels of the late 1800s, there's a whole genre of novels in which young women are having to make decisions about some, you know, repacious man who's after
turns.zh: 比如说，如果你手里还攥着「勤奋敬业」这张牌，那「口臭」这张牌也许就没那么糟了。可见把这件事教给年轻人，对父母来说有多重要。如果你去看1800年代末的小说，有一整类小说，讲年轻女性不得不针对某个贪得无厌、盯着她……

turns.en: her in some way, usually tied to money and inheritance. And you know how Zach Gallifinakis is kind of the universal sidekick in our movies today or Shrek's Tonky. Like there's always a sidekick character who's always an Arya male. In their era, it was a female, it was the female best friend of the woman who was the center of the novel.
turns.zh: ……的男人做出抉择，通常跟金钱和继承有关。你知道，就像Zach Galifianakis是当今电影里那个「万能配角」，或者《Shrek》里的Donkey那样——总会有一个配角，而且往往是男性。而在他们那个时代，这个配角是女性，是那位作为小说中心的女主角的闺蜜。

turns.en: And her best friend always ends up marrying just for love and not thinking about the financial issues. And she always ends up in a terrible situation. Like that was the kind of running joke of novels of that period. So not thinking about the finances of your marriage could get you and that's what people wanted you to understand.
turns.zh: 而她这位闺蜜最后总是只为爱情而结婚、完全不考虑财务问题，于是总是落得很糟糕的境地。这几乎就是那个时代小说里反复出现的老梗。所以，不考虑婚姻里的财务问题会让你栽跟头——这正是当时的人希望你明白的道理。

turns.en: Now it did not just mean marrying up and into more money. It meant marrying into the kind of person who you could build something with of the course of your lifetime. So at the end of the day, you're two people sitting over the kitchen table with a yellow legal pad running a small nonprofit.
turns.zh: 不过，这并不只是意味着「攀高枝、嫁/娶进更多钱」。它意味着跟那样一种人结婚：一个你可以在这一生中与之共同建立点什么的人。所以归根结底，你们两个人坐在厨房桌前，拿着一本黄色便笺本，经营着一家小型「非营利机构」。

turns.en: And you have to figure out how you're going to manage this. By the way, this still holds today. To this day, marriage is one of the strongest predictors, the quality of a marriage is one of the strongest predictors of financial outcomes that we have. And it confounds things you would not expect it to confound.
turns.zh: 你们得琢磨怎么把它经营下去。顺便说一句，这一点到今天依然成立。时至今日，婚姻——或者说一段婚姻的质量——依然是我们掌握的、对财务结果最强的预测指标之一。而且它会把一些你根本想不到会被它左右的因素也给搅进来。

turns.en: Married black men earn more than single white men. Married women at the age of 55 are earning two X, what single women at the age of 55 are earning. Married men's net worth retirement wildly outperform single men's net worth at retirement. Same sex married couples out earn heterosexuals who are single of their same age cohort.
turns.zh: 已婚黑人男性的收入高于单身白人男性。55岁的已婚女性，其收入是55岁单身女性的两倍。已婚男性退休时的净资产，大幅超越单身男性退休时的净资产。同性已婚伴侣的收入，也高于同年龄段的单身异性恋者。

turns.en: Like it's just a confounds everything you would think it wouldn't confound. So there's just something about marriage that you don't choose the family you start with. So the family you end up starting is one of the biggest things under your control. And as it turns out, marriage is a superpower because capitalism is a team sport.
turns.zh: 它就是把所有你以为不会被它左右的东西都给左右了。所以婚姻里就是有这么一种力量：你无法选择自己出身的那个家庭，但你最终组建的那个家庭，是你能掌控的最大的一件事之一。而结果证明，婚姻是一种超能力，因为资本主义是一项团队运动。

turns.en: And you just win more games playing on two-player mode. And this kind of makes sense when you think about it. Like there's risks that each of you can take that you can only take because the other one is there to cover the risks, right? There's like, you stay late at night. I'll take the kids to check me out.
turns.zh: 在「双人模式」下，你就是能赢下更多场游戏。仔细想想这挺有道理的。比如，你们各自能承担一些风险，而之所以敢承担，是因为另一方在那儿替你兜底，对吧？就像：你晚上加班晚点回，我来接孩子、照顾孩子。

turns.en: They may, they may eat Chick-fil-A, right? Like it may not, I don't know why, but I'm saying they may not eat what you would want them to eat. Just stay late and do it. You need to do to advance your career. And I'll handle this. If you compound that over the lifetime of a career, there's promotions in there you don't otherwise get.
turns.zh: 他们也许、也许会吃Chick-fil-A，对吧？也许不是你想让他们吃的东西——我不知道为什么，我是说他们可能吃得不如你意。你就安心加班，做那些为了推进事业该做的事，这边我来搞定。如果把这种情况在整段职业生涯里不断复利叠加，其中就藏着一些你原本拿不到的晋升。

turns.en: And you could see this over and over and over. For men and for women, marriage is one of the biggest predictors of financial success. Another adventure you had was investing in real estate, owning and renting out homes. And you, as a landlord, had to deal with hoarders, human traffickers, squatters.
turns.zh: 这种情况你能一遍又一遍地看到。无论对男人还是女人，婚姻都是财务成功最大的预测指标之一。你还有另一段冒险，是投资房地产、拥有并出租房屋。而作为房东，你不得不应对囤积癖、人口贩子、霸占者（squatters）。

turns.en: The FBI, does the real estate industry kind of undersell how difficult owning real estate and being a landlord really is? Oh, of course, because otherwise who would show up to the seminars? My book is not an advertisement for real estate investing, although it worked out well for me.
turns.zh: 还有FBI。房地产行业是不是有点低估了拥有房地产、当房东到底有多难？哦，当然了，因为不然的话，谁还会去参加那些研讨会呢？我的书可不是房地产投资的广告，尽管它对我而言结果很不错。

turns.en: So one of the many things, I mean, I tried so many self-experiments in this book. I Airbnb'd all the rooms in my house because believe it or not, that was how Americans paid off their mortgage. That was the primary financial advice about how to pay off your mortgage early, was to rent out rooms in your house for a long, long time.
turns.zh: 这本书里我做了太多自我实验。我把家里所有房间都挂到了Airbnb上，因为信不信由你，当年美国人就是这么还清按揭的。关于如何提前还清按揭，最主要的理财建议，就是把家里的房间出租——这条建议流行了很久很久。

turns.en: One in three Americans at any given time was a landlord from most of history, because they were trying to pay off their house. I, you know, all kinds of crazy stuff. I bought land on the moon because that was a big rage in the early space era, people like trying to claim they own the moon.
turns.zh: 在历史上的大多数时期，任何时间点都有三分之一的美国人是房东，因为他们都在想办法还清自己的房子。我还干过各种疯狂的事。我买了月球上的地，因为在早期太空时代那是股大热潮，人们争相声称自己拥有月球。

turns.en: But one of the things that comes out of World War II is you get a housing shortage. And housing shortages, believe it or not, it's hard to believe today, especially. So believe it or not, housing shortages were pretty rare in American history, because you could build a pretty fast.
turns.zh: 但二战之后出现的一个情况是住房短缺。而住房短缺——信不信由你，尤其在今天很难相信——其实在美国历史上相当罕见，因为你建房子的速度能相当快。

turns.en: But coming out of World War II, there was a housing shortage. And because of that, people who had housing, especially rental properties, did really well. And so then the first one of these to write a book about it in the 1950s, called How I became a millionaire in my spare time, becomes the best seller.
turns.zh: 但二战之后确实出现了住房短缺。正因如此，那些有房子、尤其是持有出租物业的人过得非常好。于是，1950年代第一个就此写书的人，书名叫《How I Became a Millionaire in My Spare Time》（我如何在业余时间成为百万富翁），成了畅销书。

turns.en: And people start teaching courses on real estate investing, how to get into it. That's a pretty low inflationary environment in the 50s and 60s. But then in the late 60s and 70s, inflation just explodes upwards. And so does real estate investing. And so people are rushing to try to buy a house with as little money down as possible,
turns.zh: 人们开始开设房地产投资的课程，教大家怎么入场。那可是1950、1960年代低通胀的环境。但到了60年代末和70年代，通胀猛然向上爆发，房地产投资也跟着爆发。于是人们争相用尽可能少的首付去买房子，

turns.en: and to teach other people how to do it. And by doing that, the logic is, well, if the house is going to go up by 10% just because of inflation, and you put down very little, you get the entire gain on that house. And the return on your actual invested capital is huge.
turns.zh: ……并且教别人也这么做。这么做的逻辑是：如果房子光靠通胀就要涨10%，而你首付放得很少，那你就拿到了这套房子的全部涨幅，你实际投入资本的回报率是巨大的。

turns.en: And there's this race to the bottom on this that becomes almost, not almost, becomes a darkly humorous. So that by the early 1980s, there's actually a book that sold pretty well, that told people to not only buy a house with no money down, buy it when you actually have no money in your checking account.
turns.zh: 于是一场「逐底竞赛」就此展开，变得几乎——不是几乎，是真的——一种黑色幽默。到了1980年代初，真有一本卖得还不错的书，教人们不但要零首付买房，还要在你支票账户里其实一分钱都没有的时候去买。

turns.en: But as long as you can take the closing table, they'll hand you the security deposits for the renters, the tenants, and you can rush to the bank, this is the 80s, or you're not doing this on your phone, you can rush to the bank and deposit it before your check clears.
turns.zh: 但只要你撑到交割桌（closing table）前，他们会把租客、租户的押金交到你手上，然后你就可以冲到银行去——那是80年代，你不是在手机上操作——你可以抢在你自己那张支票兑现之前，先把押金存进去。

turns.en: And then you basically kind of the check, put the money in, it's by the way illegal, can't do that. It was illegal. Then it's illegal now. Anyway, in this idea of like, I'm going to try out everything they tried then, I decided I would try little money down real estate investing, again, to try to show people what is it
turns.zh: 然后你基本上就是拿那张支票、把钱存进去——顺便说一句，这是违法的，不能那么干。当年是违法的，现在也是违法的。总之，本着「他们当年试过的每样东西我都要试一遍」的想法，我决定试试低首付的房地产投资，同样是为了向大家展示，如今去做他们当年做的事，

turns.en: like to try to do what they did now. And I tried this, of course, in the post 2008 crash. So in the early 20s, going around and real estate investing, if you look at it back today, people were like, well, duh, of course you made money. I promise you, it was not as easy as it sounded. You could find houses for really cheap.
turns.zh: ……到底是什么滋味。而我当然是在2008年崩盘之后试的这一切。所以在2020年代初四处做房地产投资，如果你今天回头看，大家会说：那还用说，你当然赚钱了。我向你保证，它并不像听起来那么容易。你能找到非常便宜的房子，

turns.en: You couldn't find people to lend you the money. And the people living in those houses, especially working class houses, were people who had their own issues that they were dealing with. And I went out to buy a house, went looking in a corridor outside of Charlotte, North Carolina,
turns.zh: ……但你找不到愿意把钱借给你的人。而住在那些房子里的人，尤其是工人阶级的房子，都是些各自都有一堆麻烦事要处理的人。我出去买房，在北卡罗来纳州Charlotte外围的一条走廊地带找，

turns.en: and I ended up buying a house and a four unit apartment building. And I came home, my wife was like, I said you could buy one. And I was like, well, it was a good deal, you know, like, I don't know, they talked me into it. And we renovated the house. And woman came out of the woodworking set. I'd love to rent it. I already own a home.
turns.zh: ……最后我买下了一栋房子和一栋四单元的公寓楼。我回到家，妻子说：「我只让你买一套啊。」我说：「呃，这买卖划算嘛，你懂的，我也不知道，是他们把我劝动的。」我们翻新了那栋房子。有个女人来看过之后说：我很想租它，我自己已经有房了，

turns.en: I just have to move for work for a few years. I was like, oh, this is great. And we never saw her again. And it turns out she worked for a temp agency that was managing the lithium mines of North Carolina where they were importing illegal labor. And so before I knew it, 40-something Haitian immigrants were living in my one-three-bedroom
turns.zh: ……只是因为工作要搬走几年。我心想：哦，太棒了。然后我们就再也没见过她。结果发现，她为一家临时人力中介工作，那家中介在管理北卡罗来纳州的锂矿，而他们在往那儿输入非法劳工。于是还没等我反应过来，四十多名海地移民就住进了我那栋三居室的……

turns.en: house. And I went to the cops, who went to the FBI, and they said, look, this is a human trafficking ring. You can evict them if you want, but we'd really appreciate if you'd let us sit on it so we could stake it out, kind of track it. And I grit my teeth. So that sounds like what I should do.
turns.zh: ……房子里。我去找了警察，警察又找了FBI，他们说：听着，这是一个人口贩卖团伙。你要是想赶他们走可以，但如果你能让我们按兵不动、好让我们蹲点监视、追踪，我们会非常感激。我咬了咬牙，说：听起来这正是我该做的。

turns.en: And before I know it, like, I'm on a conference call of the FBI, they're like a rating my rental property. By the way, all of those renovations were destroyed because you just can't have 40 people living in a house of three bedrooms. But in the apartment building, I had hoarders, which then we had rats, which meant the rats
turns.zh: 还没等我反应过来，我竟然在跟FBI开电话会议，他们好像在给我的出租物业评级。顺便说一句，那些翻新的成果全毁了，因为你根本不能让40个人住进一栋三居室的房子。而在那栋公寓楼里，我碰上了囤积癖住户，接着就有了老鼠，这意味着老鼠……

turns.en: from the hoarders were getting into the other apartments. And I had to go and I politely informed them, you can't do that here, right? Like, your neighbors are suffering because of what you're doing. And they probably pulled a shotgun on me. And I distinctly remember leaping off the steps, trying to run to my car with a shotgun
turns.zh: ……从囤积癖那户窜进了其他公寓。我不得不去，客客气气地告诉他们：这儿不能这么干，对吧？你的邻居正因为你的所作所为而受苦。而他们大概抄起一把霰弹枪对着我。我清楚地记得自己从台阶上跳下来，拼命想跑向我的车，身后一支霰弹枪……

turns.en: pointed at my back that had just a second ago been pointed at my belly. And instead of thinking about my life and my children, all I can remember was this old like rock song, give me three steps, give me three steps, mister. And I'm just like running for dear life, thinking about this old rock song my dad used to listen to.
turns.zh: ……指着我的后背，而就在前一秒它还指着我的肚子。而我脑子里想的不是我的人生、不是我的孩子，我记得的只有一首老摇滚歌：「给我三步，先生，给我三步。」（Give Me Three Steps）我就那么没命地跑，满脑子都是这首我爸过去常听的老摇滚。

turns.en: And as I'm driving away, I finally thought, I may have made a mistake. This might not be for me. But I sat down and I thought, well, this is probably as bad as real estate investing can get. So what if I run this like a business and see how, you know, what's the upside? And so over time, I just got really good at it.
turns.zh: 开车离开时，我终于想到：我可能犯了个错，这行也许不适合我。但我坐下来琢磨：好吧，房地产投资糟糕也就糟糕到这个地步了。那如果我像经营一门生意一样去经营它，看看上行空间有多大呢？于是随着时间推移，我就真的越来越擅长它了。

turns.en: It helped that I was raised by a dad who was an electrician. And though for I knew that what I owned was not homes, but what I owned was, you know, two by fours and electrical wire and pipes. And so I kind of understood intuitively what to do when things went wrong. But also I just kind of decided to eat my own cooking.
turns.zh: 我父亲是电工，这对我有帮助。所以我早就明白，我拥有的并不是「房子」，而是那些2×4的木料、电线和管道。所以东西出问题时，我几乎凭直觉就知道该怎么办。而且我也干脆决定「亲口尝尝自己做的菜」。

turns.en: What was the one lesson of history to get ahead? Concentration. And then diversify you diverse by the end of your life, not the beginning. And so I decided I'm going to go all in. I'm going to concentrate and see if I can make a million dollars. And to my great surprise, I overshot and one day looked up and was like, honey, we're
turns.zh: 历史上出人头地的那一条教训是什么？集中（concentration）。分散化（diversify）是留到人生末尾去做的事，不是开头。所以我决定全押进去，我要集中，看看自己能不能赚到一百万美元。令我大为惊讶的是，我冲过了头。有一天我抬起头来说：亲爱的，我们……

turns.en: I think we're millionaires. And then it kept going and kept going. And eventually I was able to just say, all right, I can just sit at home and write. And that was a, it was an interesting experience. I have failed upwards as an academic into a place where I never thought I'd be. Well, Amy and I have a million more questions for you.
turns.zh: ……我觉得我们成百万富翁了。然后就一路涨、一路涨。最后我总算可以说：好，我可以就待在家里写作了。那是一段很有意思的经历。作为一个学者，我算是「向上失败」，跌跌撞撞到了一个我从没想过自己会到的位置。Amy和我还有一百万个问题想问你。

turns.en: But I'm curious to find out how you see your career evolve going forward. Do you view yourself primarily as an academic, a journalist and writer, real estate investor? What do you think you'll be doing in the future? Well, thank you for having the time to have this conversation.
turns.zh: 但我很好奇，你如何看待自己未来的职业发展？你主要把自己看成学者、记者兼作家，还是房地产投资人？你觉得未来自己会做什么？嗯，谢谢你们抽时间进行这次对话。

turns.en: I think going forward, I am at some level who I've always been, which is a kid from the rural south who fell in love with history and wanted to teach other people about it.
